focus: Fold bluff catcher to an overbet
opponentAction: A value-heavy big blind overbets 30 big blinds into 24 on a blank river.
prompt: If A-10 offsuit for top pair wins only about 20% of the time, what does the new price require?
reasoning: Calling 30 to win a final pot of 84 requires about 36% equity. An estimated 20% win rate falls well short, so the same top-pair bluff catcher must be released at this larger price.
takeaway: The hand can stay the same while the bet size changes a call into a fold.

choices.label: Raise all-in
choices.feedback: A bluff raise risks the remaining stack against a polarized range that is already too value-heavy.

choices.label: Call 30 big blinds
choices.feedback: The call needs about 36% equity, far above the realistic bluff estimate for this value-heavy line.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: The disciplined fold avoids paying a 36% threshold with an estimated win rate near 20%.

opponentAction: Cutoff raises to 2.5 big blinds. You will be out of position if called.
prompt: Which size best supports the value plan with pocket queens?
reasoning: Out of position, pocket queens benefits from a larger three-bet. Eleven big blinds creates value and reduces the opener’s ability to call cheaply with a wide range.
takeaway: Use a larger three-bet out of position than in position against the same opening size.

choices.label: Raise to 11 big blinds
choices.feedback: The larger out-of-position size builds value and charges the opener for positional advantage.

choices.label: Call 2 big blinds
choices.feedback: Calling is playable, but invites the big blind and misses a clear value re-raise.

choices.label: Raise to 6 big blinds
choices.feedback: This small size gives the opener and big blind an attractive price to realize equity.

opponentAction: An active button raises to 2.5 big blinds and small blind folds.
prompt: Which aggressive plan has the best structure with A-3 suited?
reasoning: A-3 suited removes combinations of aces, ace-king, and ace-queen while retaining straight and flush potential. Those properties make it a deliberate occasional bluff three-bet.
takeaway: Choose pressure hands for blockers and playability, not simply because they are too weak to call.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: Folding is acceptable, but gives up the ace blocker and suited wheel potential.

choices.label: Call 1.5 big blinds
choices.feedback: Calling uses the price, though it does not apply immediate pressure to the wide open.

choices.label: Raise to 9 big blinds
choices.feedback: The ace blocks premium continues and the suited low card retains several ways to improve.

opponentAction: After 17 quiet hands with only one prior raise, the opponent check-raises your 16-big-blind river bet all-in. Few natural draws missed.
prompt: How should the established rare-aggression read affect top two pair on a paired river?
reasoning: top two pair on a paired river is strong in absolute terms, but the relevant evidence is a large river raise from a consistently passive range with few credible bluffs. The measured exploit is a disciplined fold.
takeaway: Against established patience, give rare large aggression more credit when the line lacks bluffs.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: The rare, large river raise and lack of missed draws make the value range too concentrated for this bluff catcher.

choices.label: Call all-in
choices.feedback: Strong absolute value does not supply enough bluffs to a line this opponent has almost never taken.

opponentAction: A disciplined under-the-gun player opens to 2.5 big blinds and every other player folds.
prompt: How should the tight opening position affect A-8 offsuit?
reasoning: The same stack that supports a reshove against a wide button open does not justify one against a tight early range. A-8 offsuit lacks enough equity when called and receives too few immediate folds.
takeaway: A reshove is a range interaction, not a stack-size reflex.

choices.label: Call 1.5 big blinds
choices.feedback: Calling consumes a meaningful share of the stack and leaves a dominated hand out of position with little postflop room.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: The early opening range and likely all-in continues dominate too much of this hand’s equity.

choices.label: Raise all-in
choices.feedback: The tight opener folds less often and calls with a range that performs very well against A-8 offsuit.

opponentAction: Big blind called modest flop and turn bets, then checks a blank river.
prompt: Which size keeps weaker one-pair hands calling against K-J offsuit?
reasoning: K-J offsuit remains ahead of several natural bluff catchers on a blank river. A small value bet is sized for those worse calls instead of isolating against the top of the range.
takeaway: Thin value succeeds by giving weaker hands a price they can realistically pay.

choices.label: Bet 10 big blinds
choices.feedback: The inviting size targets weaker one-pair hands without forcing the range to become too strong.

choices.label: Check back
choices.feedback: Checking guarantees showdown, but misses value from worse top pairs and stubborn lower pairs.

choices.label: Bet 48 big blinds
choices.feedback: The overbet folds many hands you beat and is more likely to be called by a stronger range.

opponentAction: Big blind bets 16 big blinds into 16 big blinds. Nine flush outs are about 19% with one card to come.
prompt: What does the price say about continuing?
reasoning: Calling 16 big blinds creates a 48 big blinds final pot, so the break-even price is 33%. The stated 19% draw chance is not enough.
takeaway: Strong-looking draws can still be folds when a large wager offers the wrong price.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: The call needs 33% equity, well above the stated 19% chance to complete the flush.

choices.label: Call 16 big blinds
choices.feedback: A visually strong draw is still a losing call when its equity is below the direct price.

choices.label: Raise all-in
choices.feedback: A bluff raise needs credible fold equity; the draw alone does not erase the bad price.

opponentAction: A disciplined under-the-gun player moves all-in and every other player folds.
prompt: Does the posted big blind make K-7 offsuit a profitable call?
reasoning: The all-in came from the earliest seat, so the shoving range should be much stronger than a button range. K-7 offsuit is frequently dominated, and the slightly better price cannot repair that equity gap.
takeaway: An all-in call needs direct equity; chips already posted do not justify calling a range that dominates you.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: The early shoving range dominates too many combinations, and the posted blind does not supply enough equity.

choices.label: Call all-in
choices.feedback: Calling has no fold equity and puts the remaining stack against a range that is much stronger than this hand.

opponentAction: Two places advance. You are the shortest stack, action folds to you, and both blinds can eliminate you.
prompt: Should bubble fear stop the first-in opportunity with A-6 suited?
reasoning: As the shortest stack, you have less survival value to protect and cannot depend on another player busting first. A-6 suited is strong enough to use late-position fold equity now.
takeaway: Bubble pressure can tighten calls while leaving good short-stack first-in shoves intact.

choices.label: Move all-in
choices.feedback: A-6 suited combines useful equity with the chance to win the blinds immediately while acting first.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: Waiting gives the blinds a larger share of the remaining stack and removes this hand’s first-in fold equity.

opponentAction: Big blind bets 20 big blinds into 16 big blinds. You estimate this bluff catcher wins 27% of the time.
prompt: What does the price tell you to do?
reasoning: Calling 20 big blinds makes the final pot 56 big blinds. Required equity is 20 ÷ 56 ≈ 36%, above the stated 27% win estimate.
takeaway: Do not let absolute hand strength override the price and your range-based estimate.

choices.label: Raise all-in
choices.feedback: Turning showdown value into a bluff needs blocker and fold evidence you do not have.

choices.label: Call 20 big blinds
choices.feedback: Top pair looks attractive, but the call loses when your equity estimate is below the price.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: You need about 36% equity, so a trustworthy 27% estimate cannot support a call.

opponentAction: Two places advance. The 42-big-blind leader shoves from the button, you are second in chips, and a 6-big-blind stack remains.
prompt: How should bubble risk change the marginal call with pocket sevens?
reasoning: The leader covers you and the shortest stack is under immediate blind pressure. pocket sevens is not far enough ahead of the shoving range to justify risking elimination for a marginal chip gain.
takeaway: Covered middle stacks should tighten close all-in calls while a much shorter stack remains.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: Preserving the second stack while a six-big-blind player remains outweighs a thin chip-equity call.

choices.label: Call all-in
choices.feedback: pocket sevens may be close in chip terms, but calling has no fold equity and losing ends the event before the shortest stack.

opponentAction: Big blind calls the flop, then checks the turn.
prompt: How should you handle second pair with a strong kicker?
reasoning: Second pair has useful showdown value but does not clearly gain from a large bet. Position lets you take a free card and make the river decision with more information.
takeaway: A good check can protect medium-strength showdown value; aggression always needs a purpose.

choices.label: Check back
choices.feedback: Checking realizes your showdown value and avoids building a large pot against stronger pairs.

choices.label: Bet 12 big blinds
choices.feedback: A pot-sized bet isolates this medium-strength hand against too much of the stronger range.

choices.label: Bet 4 big blinds
choices.feedback: A small protection bet can be mixed, but many worse hands fold while stronger hands continue.

opponentAction: You act first with five live ranges still behind.
prompt: Does the short stack make K-7 offsuit an automatic all-in?
reasoning: Short-stack urgency does not erase position. K-7 offsuit must pass five ranges and performs poorly when called, so preserving the remaining stack is better than forcing an early all-in.
takeaway: Keep an early-position fold range even when the stack is short.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: The hand is too often dominated or called by stronger ranges after passing five players.

choices.label: Call 1 big blind
choices.feedback: Open-limping spends scarce chips without creating fold pressure or a clear response to a raise.

choices.label: Move all-in
choices.feedback: Five players can wake up with stronger hands, making this shove too loose for a practical baseline.

opponentAction: A wide button opener raises to 2.2 big blinds and the small blind folds.
prompt: Which response gets the clearest value from A-K offsuit?
reasoning: A-K offsuit performs strongly against both a wide button open and a reasonable calling range. With fewer than twenty big blinds, the direct reshove avoids an awkward small three-bet and captures the dead money.
takeaway: Strong hands can reshove for value against wide late-position opens when the stack is already compact.

choices.label: Call 1.2 big blinds
choices.feedback: Calling keeps the range wide, but gives up immediate value and lets the opener realize equity.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: A-K offsuit is far ahead of a wide button opening range and too strong to release.

choices.label: Raise all-in
choices.feedback: The reshove wins the dead money now or enters the all-in with strong equity against the button’s continue range.

opponentAction: Early position raises to 2.5 big blinds. You are 100 big blinds deep and the blinds are passive.
prompt: Which response best uses pocket fives?
reasoning: pocket fives flops a set infrequently, so it needs deep stacks, a manageable price, and a good chance to realize its implied value.
takeaway: Set-mine only when the price, stack depth, position, and players behind support the future payoff.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: Folding avoids variance, but the deep stacks and position make a call viable.

choices.label: Raise to 8 big blinds
choices.feedback: A re-raise can mix, but it often folds worse hands and faces strong continues.

choices.label: Call 2.5 big blinds
choices.feedback: Deep stacks and position provide enough upside when you flop a set.

opponentAction: Action folds to you. The button and both blinds remain.
prompt: What is the cleanest first-in action with K-J suited?
reasoning: K-J suited combines enough card quality and position to open profitably from the cutoff. A consistent 2.5-big-blind size keeps the strategy clear.
takeaway: Open more hands as fewer players remain, but enter with a raise rather than a limp.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: K-J suited is strong enough to enter from the cutoff after earlier players fold.

choices.label: Call 1 big blind
choices.feedback: Open-limping gives up immediate pressure and invites a crowded pot.

choices.label: Raise to 2.5 big blinds
choices.feedback: A consistent small raise builds value and can win the blinds.

opponentAction: Two places advance. A 4-big-blind button folded, and the 45-big-blind leader waits in the big blind.
prompt: What is the cleanest baseline with a marginal K-6 offsuit?
reasoning: K-6 offsuit sits near the normal opening boundary, but this specific stack configuration adds a meaningful survival cost. The leader covers you and the four-big-blind player may be forced all-in soon.
takeaway: Name the shorter stack and the covering stack before making a bubble-tight fold.

choices.label: Move all-in
choices.feedback: Risking the entire medium stack through the leader is unnecessary while the shortest stack is nearly blinded out.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: The hand is marginal, the leader can apply maximum pressure, and a four-big-blind stack remains.

choices.label: Raise to 2.2 big blinds
choices.feedback: The open invites a re-shove from the covering leader in a spot where your range cannot defend comfortably.

opponentAction: Big blind called the flop, both players checked the turn, and big blind checks when the third flush card arrives.
prompt: Which bluff size best uses the blocker carried by A-5 offsuit with the nut-suit blocker?
reasoning: A-5 offsuit with the nut-suit blocker has little showdown value, blocks the nut flush, and does not block many one-pair folds. Those properties make it a more credible large bluff than a random missed hand.
takeaway: Choose river bluffs that block calls and leave likely folds in the opponent’s range.

choices.label: Bet 36 big blinds
choices.feedback: The polarized size pressures one-pair hands while the nut-suit blocker removes important strong calls.

choices.label: Check back
choices.feedback: Giving up is acceptable, but it does not use the nut-suit blocker against a capped checking range.

choices.label: Bet 8 big blinds
choices.feedback: A small bet gives many pairs and low flushes an easy bluff-catching price.

opponentAction: Big blind called your flop bet and checks after a turn that improves connected calling hands.
prompt: Does K-Q offsuit still have enough equity and fold pressure to barrel?
reasoning: K-Q offsuit has little realistic improvement equity and the turn strengthens many flop calls. Without useful blockers or credible folds, a second bluff spends chips without a strong route to win.
takeaway: Give up when the turn removes both improvement equity and believable fold equity.

choices.label: Check back
choices.feedback: Checking gives up cleanly when the hand has little improvement equity and the caller’s range strengthens.

choices.label: Bet 9 big blinds
choices.feedback: The called flop and connecting turn leave too few better hands likely to fold to another routine bet.

choices.label: Bet 27 big blinds
choices.feedback: Increasing the size does not repair poor equity, weak blockers, and a turn that favors the caller.

opponentAction: The short button moves all-in after the small blind folds. You already posted the big blind.
prompt: What does a wide late-position shove support with A-Q offsuit?
reasoning: The button can shove widely with only two opponents and a very short stack. A-Q offsuit remains strong against that range, and the big blind already in the pot improves the call price.
takeaway: Call short late-position shoves wider with hands that retain clear equity against the full shoving range.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: A-Q offsuit is too strong against a wide late-position shoving range to surrender the posted blind and pot.

choices.label: Call all-in
choices.feedback: The hand has strong equity against the button’s wide short-stack range and receives a price improved by the posted blind.

opponentAction: Big blind bets 8 big blinds into 24 on a three-flush river. The nut flush remains possible.
prompt: How should J-10 suited for a jack-high flush continue without folding out the bluffs it beats?
reasoning: J-10 suited for a jack-high flush is strong enough to continue, but a raise has poor value targeting: worse hands often fold and better flushes continue. Calling preserves the opponent’s bluffs and controls the final pot.
takeaway: Before raising the river, name worse hands that can actually call the raise.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: Folding is cautious, but gives up too much against a small bet containing weaker value and bluffs.

choices.label: Call 8 big blinds
choices.feedback: Calling keeps bluffs and weaker flushes in while limiting losses to the nut-heavy part of the range.

choices.label: Raise to 28 big blinds
choices.feedback: Raising folds many worse hands and is most likely to receive action from higher flushes.

focus: Folding dominated hands to a three-bet
opponentAction: You opened to 2.5 big blinds. Small blind three-bets to 11 big blinds and big blind folds.
prompt: How should you respond with K-Q offsuit?
reasoning: K-Q offsuit is offsuit, frequently dominated, and faces a large out-of-position re-raise. The 2.5 big blinds already invested do not make an unprofitable continue correct.
takeaway: Treat the open as sunk cost; continue only when the hand survives the new range and price.

choices.label: Move all-in
choices.feedback: A shove is usually called by a range with substantially better equity.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: Release the dominated offsuit hand instead of defending the earlier opening investment.

choices.label: Call 8.5 big blinds
choices.feedback: This hand makes too many second-best pairs against the stronger three-bet range.

opponentAction: Everyone folds to you. You have posted 0.5 big blinds.
prompt: What is the simplest value-first plan with pocket sevens?
reasoning: pocket sevens is ahead of a random big-blind holding. Raising builds value even though you will act first after the flop.
takeaway: When folded to the small blind, attack with solid hands while respecting the postflop position disadvantage.

choices.label: Call 0.5 big blinds
choices.feedback: Some strategies limp, but raising is the clearer beginner baseline with this hand.

choices.label: Raise to 3 big blinds
choices.feedback: Raise for value and make the big blind pay to continue in position.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: pocket sevens is too strong to surrender against one random big-blind range.

opponentAction: Button raises to 2.5 big blinds and small blind folds. Effective stacks are 30 big blinds.
prompt: Which plan uses the shorter stack best with pocket jacks?
reasoning: At 30 big blinds, pocket jacks has strong equity against both the button open and a reasonable continuing range. A compact three-bet creates a low stack-to-pot ratio and a clear commitment plan.
takeaway: As stacks shorten, decide whether the value three-bet will continue against an all-in before raising.

choices.label: Raise to 8.5 big blinds
choices.feedback: The efficient size builds value and prepares to continue against a shove at this stack depth.

choices.label: Call 1.5 big blinds
choices.feedback: Calling is playable, but misses value and lets the button realize equity cheaply.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: pocket jacks is far too strong to fold against a wide button opening range.

opponentAction: You three-bet preflop, cutoff called, and now checks this connected flop.
prompt: How should the board interaction change the plan with A-K offsuit?
reasoning: The caller’s condensed range connects strongly with this low, coordinated flop. A-K offsuit retains future equity but lacks the nut advantage required for a large automatic continuation bet.
takeaway: Three-betting preflop does not guarantee postflop range control on connected boards.

choices.label: Bet 7 big blinds
choices.feedback: A small bet can mix with better blockers, but this hand does not need to force immediate pressure.

choices.label: Check back
choices.feedback: Checking preserves overcard equity and avoids inflating a pot on a board rich in strong calls and raises.

choices.label: Bet 21 big blinds
choices.feedback: The caller owns many pairs, two pair, sets, and draws that can continue or raise against a large bet.

focus: Bluff catch at a fair price
opponentAction: Big blind leads 8 big blinds into 24 on a blank river after several natural draws miss.
prompt: If A-J offsuit for top pair wins about 28% of the time, what does the price support?
reasoning: Calling 8 to win a final pot of 40 requires 20% equity. The estimated 28% win rate clears that threshold, so calling is the price-aware baseline without overplaying the hand.
takeaway: Small river bets can justify bluff catches when enough missed draws remain.

choices.label: Call 8 big blinds
choices.feedback: The call needs 20% equity and the plausible missed draws support an estimate above that price.

choices.label: Raise to 28 big blinds
choices.feedback: Turning a profitable bluff catcher into a raise folds bluffs and receives action from stronger value.

choices.label: Fold
choices.feedback: Folding gives up when the estimated win rate exceeds the 20% break-even threshold.

opponentAction: You raised preflop and both button and big blind called. Both opponents check this flop.
prompt: What changes now that two ranges must continue against Q-J offsuit?
reasoning: Multiway, each opponent can continue more selectively while the combined field connects more often. Q-J offsuit has useful overcards but not enough range support for automatic pressure.
takeaway: Bluff less multiway because one bet must work through several continuing ranges.

choices.label: Check back
choices.feedback: Checking preserves overcard equity and respects that at least one of two callers connects more often.

choices.label: Bet 3 big blinds
choices.feedback: A small bet can mix selectively, but needs stronger blockers or backdoor equity against two ranges.

choices.label: Bet 9 big blinds
choices.feedback: A pot-sized bluff must force folds from two ranges on a coordinated board, making the risk too high.
